newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl refuses to be drawn on Spain's EMU entry.
newsitem.headline: Kohl refuses to be drawn on Spain's EMU entry.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl gave support on Thursday to Spanish efforts to join the European Union's planned single currency, rejecting the idea that Bonn was fundamentally opposed but declining to say if Spain should be admitted from the start.

Kohl was speaking to reporters after talks with Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar, two days after a top German official said some countries which qualified for European Monetary Union (EMU) should stay outside for a time after 1999.

While Aznar said Spain's progress towards joining EMU was "irreversible", and backed up by its economic data, Kohl said no decision would be made before early 1998, on the basis of the terms set down in the Maastricht Treaty.
"I'm watching with great interest and sympathy the enormous efforts made by the Spanish government," Kohl said.
But he added that the decision on who to admit to EMU and when was not one for Germany to make, particularly as Germany itself did not currently fulfil the Maastricht criteria.
"It's something everyone must achieve for themselves...I'll be happy enough if we've done our own homework by D-day."

Both Kohl and Aznar said the question had not even come up in their discussions. Spanish delegation sources said beforehand that Aznar and his cabinet were hoping for acknowledgement from Bonn that their austerity budget and structural reforms had put them on course to join the first wave of EMU entrants.

Such assurances seemed unlikely to be given after German Finance Ministry number two Juergen Stark made clear on Tuesday Bonn was worried some countries did not have the track record to show they could maintain economic stability after joining EMU.

Stark did not name any countries, but there was little doubt he was aiming at southern European EU members such as Spain and Italy when he told a conference of newspaper editors that some countries which qualify on paper "would be well advised to maintain exchange rate flexibility for a certain period".
In an interview in the weekly Die Zeit, Aznar reacted crossly to the idea that Spain could fall into this category.
"Spain must be and will be one of the founders of monetary union," he said.
"Do (the Germans) really think we Spanish want a weak currency? We want exactly what the Germans want: a strong euro."

While Madrid has garnered popular support for its EMU drive with the carrot of joining the EU elite on equal terms, Bonn has to calm Germans' fears that they may end up baling out the deficits of countries less committed to budget discipline.
But Kohl was keen to play down suggestions that Germany had any prejudices against Spanish membership of EMU, or that it was working towards an EU of first-class and second-class members.

His insistence on observing the letter of the Maastricht Treaty was in line with Spain's own demand that those who fulfil those conditions in 1997 must be allowed to join EMU without question in 1999.
"I believe last year about eight or nine million Germans went to Spain with all their prejudices, to lie in the sun and eat and drink," he said.

"They didn't spend all day wondering whether the restaurant had a copy of the EU guidelines hanging in the kitchen, they felt good and came home content. If that's how these prejudices are worked off, then I've got no objection to that." REUTER
